en: *Ātmasādhanāvatāra* (Introduction to the Realization of the Self):

In that glorious [mind], which is free from the impurities of all eight conceptual constructions, this entire world— which arises from conceptualization and is of its nature— does not abide within the mind.
Having bowed to that state of ultimate bliss for embodied beings— which is attained through the method of the mental continuum of one's own nature—
the severance of the entanglement of the succession of births shall now be fully explained.

This entire nature, which is exclusively characterized by immeasurable suffering, consists of nothing other than its connection with mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Since nirvāṇa is simply the cessation of that experience of existence (*saṃsāra*), which is of the nature of a succession from one moment to the next, one should exert oneself in order to achieve it.
For apart from conceptual construction, there exists no such thing as what is called "saṃsāra."
Therefore, for one who is free from conceptual construction, there is always the cessation of existence (bhava-nirvṛti).

If it is asked: "How can cyclic existence, which appears in the form of the apprehended object and so forth, be of the nature of mere conceptual construction? [The answer is: No, because the object of cognition is not established as being the apprehended object and so forth. Indeed, apart from the appearance of forms and the like, no other apprehended object or apprehending subject is perceived. Furthermore, that whose essential nature is not cognized cannot be the object of the conventional usage of "existence," for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, there can be no cognition of that [object] without a cognition of its connection [with the subject], because for anyone, such a connection is not established through the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it is argued that pleasure (*sātā*) and so forth, appearing internally, possess the status of the grasper (*grāhaka*), whereas blue and so forth, characterized by appearing as external to that [subject], possess the status of the grasped (*grāhya*); [we reply: no, because no causal operation (*vyāpāra*) is established between pleasure and so forth and blue and so forth. Moreover, something whose operation is not cognized cannot be called a grasper; for if that were the case, it would follow that even external things like color-form (*rūpa*) would be graspers.
For we do not perceive any cause for a fixed distinction such that, when two things appear simultaneously and independently, one is the apprehended object and the other is the apprehending subject.

The thought "I perceive blue and so forth" is also merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*), because there is a cognition of things appearing internally and externally with independence. Indeed, this entire continuum of conceptual constructions such as the "grasper" (*grāhaka*) and so on is intent upon manifesting independent experience, since it exists only when things appear while devoid of any activity of mutual grasping. Thus, what could possibly be the grasper of anything? Accordingly, it has been said: "For, Subhūti, one dharma does not know another dharma," and so forth.

As for what was stated—that forms are cognized by two types of consciousness, and so forth—that is not a fault, because it is based merely upon the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of those forms, similar to the occasional teaching of a "person" (*pudgala*) and so on.

[Objection: Let it be then that the world has the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and lacks a substantial self (*anātman*), beginning with such an approach. [Response: No, because consciousness itself is devoid of a nature that is either one or many.

For it is thus: that [consciousness] is not one, because its perception is variegated due to the distinctions of blue and so forth; and because even a single color, such as white, appears with distinctions of beginning, middle, and end; and because there is a distinction in the utility of its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Furthermore, being manifold is characterized by nothing more than this. Nor is it manifold, because parts consisting of the appearance of white and so forth are not perceived through the conceptualization of atoms (*paramāṇu*). And there is no other mode apart from being one or many, because these two are mutually exclusive by virtue of their nature as mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

If it is asked: "But if all things are entirely devoid of self-nature (*nirātmaka*), from where does this observed difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) arise? [The reply is: It has already been explained that, for those whose nature is not investigated, there is no cognition of anything other than that which arises solely from preceding conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*).

If it is argued: "Let it be then that the reality of all entities exists precisely as entities, because the nature of being a real thing (*vastutva*) is defined by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)," [we reply: no, for there is no contradiction in accepting existence based on mere appearance in that context. Selflessness (*nairātmya*) is established precisely through the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics; it is not, however, because of the impairment of appearance. As it has been said: "Subhūti, form is not one thing and emptiness another; rather, form itself is empty of the characteristic of form," and so forth. (PraPā xx) [End of quotation].

For this very reason, because all conventional entities appear through the distinction of preceding and succeeding [moments], their permanence is not to be suspected. As for that which was said: "O Sons of the Victor, that which is called the triple world is representation-only" (*Daśabhūmikasūtra* 20), that was for the purpose of dispelling the determination of external objects by those who are deeply attached to internal existence. Since, when that [external object] exists, it is possible to easily effect the refutation of even the determination of mind-only.
Thus he says: "Relying upon mind-only, the external nature of the knowable is to be understood."
Abiding in the focal point of suchness, one should transcend mind-only.
Therefore, the birth of beings— which consists of conceptual constructions such as "I" and "mine"— is contradicted by the vision of selflessness in the manner just explained.

In order to deliver those beings who have fallen under the power of others through their distortions, one should first direct oneself toward the very emptiness of all phenomena, having generated the intention of supreme compassion.

For instance, a continuous stream of wholesome qualities such as giving—whether produced by the perception of a recipient and so forth, or even brought about by compassion—is not capable, in the slightest degree, of accomplishing the state free from conceptual construction regarding self and other. This is because a distorted determination is the cause for the arising of conceptualizations corresponding to itself. And thus it has been said:
Without wisdom, these five perfections are eyeless;
lacking a guide, they do not aspire toward awakening.

However, because it consists of the ascertainment of the selflessness of all things, even though it is itself conceptual in nature, its very essence is the ascertainment of its own object; thus, through all forms of conceptualization, there is indeed the cessation of ordinary cognition. Furthermore, that which has once been observed to contradict something else will, through extreme habituation, completely eliminate its opposite—just as fire eliminates cold and the like. Otherwise, if there were doubt regarding the contrary in every case, practical activity would be impossible.
And it is said in this regard:

If one examines phenomena as being without self, and having examined them, one should cultivate that [insight], it is the cause for attaining the fruit of nirvāṇa; whatever other cause there may be, it does not lead to liberation.

Since one who lacks the distinction of skillful means is unable to produce the omniscient gnosis—which is free from the stains of all conceptual construction and benefits the entire world—one must therefore strive to bring about the presence of superior skillful means.

For the omniscient gnosis is characterized by its capacity to benefit the entire world without exception; and such benefit arises from unsurpassed magnanimity, the cause of which is precisely the practice of [the realization of] selflessness (*nairātmya*), because the fruit of that practice is the abandonment of mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*). As it is said:
"From both magnanimity and profundity, there is maturation and non-conceptuality;
In this teaching of these two, that means is unsurpassed."

Therefore, let it be that the functioning of the volition of giving and so forth, when free from error, is the means for the transformation into omniscience, because such [volition] constitutes the cause of perfect enlightenment. And thus it has been said:
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, as well as vigor,
the meditative concentrations, and wisdom— these are dedicated toward supreme enlightenment.
And one should not grasp at the signs of the aggregates of awakening;
thus, this should not be taught to those who are beginners.

This is not so; for the practice of dissimilar causes is not conducive to being the direct cause of perfect awakening (*sambodhi*). Indeed, the fruit—which consists of vastness and profundity—is to be realized as having the nature of the self, yet the cause here does not possess that nature. This is because the volition regarding giving and so forth is generally directed toward objects that are not vast in nature; and because aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), by virtue of having as its object the majesty of a perfectly awakened one occurring at an extremely remote time, does not serve as an antidote to the conceptualization of a non-vast self-nature.

For the ordinary nature (*prākṛta-svarūpa*) is to be abandoned by one who possesses an excellence of compassion, because it fails to benefit immeasurable beings. And even while its antidote—the mental states consisting of giving and so forth, which constitute the equipment of the vow—is active, how can there be confidence that this [ordinary nature], whose momentum has not yet ceased, will be turned back at some future time? For no such kind of thing is observed to exist within the determination of profundity when its own opposite has been destroyed.

For selflessness, when cultivated elsewhere apart from the self, does not bring about a state of being that is free from the stain of conceptual construction; for it does not function because it is opposed to the conceptualization of its own nature. However, when the emptiness of forms such as the subject (*grāhaka*) is made manifest through the non-differentiation from one's own mind—

Then, being perceived at that very moment as the antidote to all unreal conceptual constructions, it will—through the intensification of the practice of cultivation—produce the state in which all mental fabrications have been eliminated; thus, it would become an object of engagement for those who act with foresight.

However, the aspiration such as "May I become a Buddha" is not directly the antidote to the appearance of a non-noble self; rather, it is the cause for attaining the state of a Perfectly Awakened One. As it is said: "How, noble son, will you realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, since you undertake all these difficult feats while remaining ignorant of the reality of all Tathāgatas?
Therefore, one should cultivate nobility just like selflessness, as being entirely inseparable from its own intrinsic nature.

If it is asked: "But how can that which is non-existent, even when cultivated, be capable of bringing about the attainment of the desired result?"—that is not so; for even that which has not [previously] existed becomes the cause of a vivid appearance through the practice of cultivation, just like the magical transformation of earth and so forth.

And how is it unreal? If you say: because it is a mental engagement consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manaskāra*), since it functions by superimposing that form upon one's own self which is devoid of the form of the Buddha’s body.

In that case, even the mental attention (*manaskāra*) directed toward reality would not be "actual" (*bhūta*), because it does not proceed in accordance with reality as it is. For reality has the sole characteristic of being non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), whereas that mental attention does not function in that manner; rather, in the stage of a beginner, it proceeds in the form of conceptualization. Let it be that it possesses conceptualization; nevertheless, since things are determined by it according to their actual state as they truly exist, its status as "mental attention directed toward reality" is established.

However, another [type of attention], which superimposes an entirely different nature upon this [object], is designated as "attention consisting of resolute conviction" (*adhimukti-manaskāra*). This is because it attends to the form of the Best of Sages—which, like reality (*tattva*), is actually non-existent—within the ordinary self. This is not so. For the attention consisting of selflessness (*nairātmya-manaskāra*) takes as its object the nature of things exactly as they are; it would attend either to those things that appear as having the status of being its own objects, or to those produced by the domain of erroneous conceptualization.

In that regard, if the former position holds, it applies equally elsewhere: even the mental engagement consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manaskāra*) proceeds only by grasping the aspect (*ākāra*) that constitutes its own object; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of resolute conviction. For a cognition that does not apprehend the aspect of its own object is not the referent for the conventional usage of "resolute conviction," since the defining characteristic of all cognitions is the perception of the aspect recognized as their own object.

Now, as for the second position: that too is untenable. Because the object of the apprehension of the grasper (*grāhaka-adhyavasāya*) is not made an object by the cognition of selflessness (*nairātmya-pratyaya*). For there is no other so-called "object" apart from the cognition itself by which another could make it its object; this has been explained at length previously, like the mental attention to reality (*tattva-manaskāra*). Since its object is merely its own internal form (*svākāra-mātra*), there is no lack of existence for one who is resolved upon the vastness (*audārya-adhimukta*).

Furthermore, this [mental application] does not function as a superimposition of a sublime form upon the ordinary self, because the ordinary form has not been made an object through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) by way of the form of the body of a perfectly awakened Buddha; and because superimposition is impossible with respect to that which is not an object. For the nature of the ordinary consists in the characteristic of appearing as an ordinary conceptual construction, whereas mental application has as its domain the form of the Sugata, which possesses excellence and does not manifest in that [ordinary] form.

If it does not superimpose any other form upon its own non-sublime nature, how can it be its antidote? [The answer is: because the mental attention (*manaskāra*) that manifests the Sugata-form arises by its very nature as something extraordinary, and because, through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it becomes the cause for the arising of a continuous and perfectly clear cognition of the same kind.

Furthermore, at the time when a sublime cognition arises, no other cognition with an ordinary form as its object is experienced. Nor can it be determined that such an ordinary intrinsic nature exists even though it is not being perceived, because—as has already been largely established—its very nature consists solely in being perceived.
Therefore, one partakes of enlightenment only by meditating upon oneself as Samantabhadra, whose conceptual constructions have been dispelled and who radiates light in all directions.
As it says:
By means of this procedure for the mudrās, even that state of perfect buddhahood which is unattainable through tens of millions of incalculable eons is attained in this very life.
Therefore, I shall explain that [process] up to the yoga with one's own presiding deity; hence, one should meditate upon the Self alone.

It is precisely with reference to such mental engagement (*manaskāra*) that the Blessed Ones—who possess the excellence of perfected gnosis—describe an equality even with one whose yoga regarding reality is not yet perfected; for, due to their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in the nature of a Perfectly Awakened One, perfected yogins do not perceive any difference [between themselves and the Buddha]. For if they were to perceive such a difference, there would be no mental engagement with the mind of a Sugata, since the Blessed Ones are characterized by the determination that there is no distinction from the *praṇa* (the vital breath/principle).

Furthermore, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines the essential nature of the Blessed Ones—who appear in various forms—to be something different from that [nature] could not have a faultless result.
Having established that infinite form of the Jina within himself as if in his own mind, he,
whose body is pure and whose supreme intellect is equal to all Buddhas, [proceeds].

It may be for the sake of accomplishing the desires of all beings without exception. And yet, even while bringing before one’s mind the Self—who is garlanded with a face of shimmering, immeasurable rays; who is the supreme means by virtue of being the locus of infinite fulfillment of the welfare of oneself and others; and who is anxious to never be separated from the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*)—if one does not attain the entirety of the desired perfections, then one must ensure that the mind is not mistaken regarding His true nature. This is because stainless perfection originates from wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*).

And although these two are characterized solely by the arising of a non-erroneous and noble mind, the conventional distinction between them exists due to a difference in their determinative functions (*adhyavasāya*). For instance: within that very same mind, there is error; whereas the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of wisdom (*prajñā*) consists in the exclusion of the nature of such error. However, the exclusion of the incapacity for one's own function constitutes the state of being a means (*upāya*). Thus, the limb of wisdom (*prajñāṅga*)—[hidden]—is the perfection of the savoring of supreme delight.
The wise person should constantly meditate upon that very nature which serves as the correct means for it.
Thereafter:
Through the emanations of wisdom and means, which arise as an inseparable flow of objective manifestations,
and through the objects that abide as appearances.
One should honor one's own body with misfortunes.

Bringing his own nature—which consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*)—into manifestation according to the sequence described, he should bring it face-to-face for the sake of accomplishing mastery over as many emanations (*nirmāṇa*) as there may be. To that extent, one should recognize the state of non-differentiation from that essential nature. This is because, in their capacity to arise with a seemingly inverted nature, they possess the single characteristic of consisting of wisdom and skillful means, and because they have the nature of an undivided continuum (*santati*). For a continuum is indeed a succession of conceptualizations produced by preceding volitions (*saṃkalpa*);
and what is called an "emanation" is nothing other than that very volition.

Because it possesses a manifold nature due to distinctions such as color and so forth, one might ask: "How can there be unity? If that were the case, then unity would not exist anywhere at all; for even the form of a single deity consists of multiple natures and is therefore manifold in essence. Furthermore, a partless entity is not perceived. Just as permanence is established in one place, so too is it established in other forms that possess manifold natures.

And because all [cognition] proceeds through the non-differentiated determination of the mental engagement (*manaskāra*) as "I," in dependence upon the determination of that specific form; by this, the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the equality of all entities is explained, since the absence of forms such as the subject (*grāhaka*) is equal everywhere. Furthermore, nothing that has become the locus of conventional usage is other than those objects which consist of the nature of its own appearance; for it is impossible to effect a distinction based on a nature perceived simultaneously, and it has already been established that there is no other defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, this notion that "I am equal to all" is purely conventional and intent upon the contemplation of the true nature of things as they are; it functions, but not in reality. Furthermore, nothing can be made an object of cognition as either different from or non-different from anything else, because all cognitions are restricted to their own intrinsic nature and lack the apprehension of the nature of another. And since no object has been made an object of cognition, the linguistic usage of "difference" and so forth is untenable.

Thus, for yogins, the arising of one's own mind should be contemplated as having the nature of all the maṇḍala deities, by way of its form being turned away from all opposing factors (*vipakṣa*). This is because their respective meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) indicate the non-perception of those opposites. Therefore, it is established that this alone is the uncommon cause of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
For whatever is the nature of the mind, that very thing is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, because it is free from aspects such as grasping and so forth.
Because it is luminous when adventitious stains have been removed,
and because it is the very cause for generating other types of primordial wisdom, it has the nature of mirror-like primordial wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

Because it consists of compassion and so forth that are without an objective support, and because there is no conceptualization of difference within the continuum of others, it is the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*);
because it is non-erroneous regarding all objects of knowledge, it is the knowledge of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*);
and because it is the cause for the gateway to the welfare of the entire world, it has the nature of the knowledge of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

Therefore, these are, respectively, the natures of the lords such as the Permanent One and so forth. By way of being the antidote to objective apprehension, they have the characteristic of emptiness, which is a door to liberation; and likewise, by way of being the antidotes to signs, perverted aspirations, and perverted formative activities, they are, respectively, signlessness and...
They are of the nature of liberation that is wishless and without volitional engagement.

Therefore, they are respectively the nature of the consorts of the families, such as Vajrasattvī and so forth; because they take the dharmadhātu as their object through the four doors of liberation—emptiness and so on—they are the very cause for the arising of all meditative absorptions (samādhis).
Internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) is so called because it is contrary to the inversion regarding the internal.
External emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) results from the departure from the apprehension of external objects such as form and the rest.
Internal-and-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) has as its essential nature the non-apprehension of the body that serves as the basis for those two.
Because it is free from attachment to the world of the vessel, it has the characteristic of great emptiness.

Therefore, it is the nature of the meditative absorptions (samādhi) of Vajrasattva and others, which rely upon the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna). This is because the mirror-like wisdom—the transformation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth—is the very basis for the non-apprehension of internal objects and so on; thus, by way of being the respective antidotes to their own respective distortions (*viparyāsa*).
Because it is the cause for the arising of the mind of awakening, for drawing [beings] forth, for following with affection, and for saying "well done."
Even regarding the knowledge of emptiness, it is the "emptiness of emptiness" because it is signless.
It is the "emptiness of the ultimate" because there is no grasping at signs of the ultimate.
It is the "emptiness of the conditioned" because there is no apprehension of signs in the accumulation of conditioned merit.

Because it does not engage even with the unconditioned equipment for awakening (*asaṃskṛtabodhisambhāra*), and because of its non-apprehension (*anudgraha*), there is the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā*).

Therefore, the wheel of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) has the nature of the four [vajras], such as the vajra-jewel and so forth. This is because the wisdom of equality, which consists in the transformation of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), is devoid of the apprehension of signs (*nimittagraha*) as previously explained, by way of its grasping and so forth.

This is because it serves as the cause for bestowing empowerment by way of abandoning each respective discordant factor, for increasing majesty, and for engaging with and inspiring enthusiasm for the perfection of generosity.
The emptiness of the ultimate is due to the lack of attachment to the vow for the welfare of sentient beings.

The emptiness of that which is without beginning or end is due to the non-grasping of the vow: "I must not abandon cyclic existence, which is without beginning or end. The emptiness of non-dispersal is due to the lack of attachment to the thought: "I must not scatter my roots of virtue even in the nirvana without remainder."
Because there is no aspiration such as "I must purify the lineage (*gotra*) characterized by primordial nature (*prakṛti*)," there is the emptiness of primordial nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).

Therefore, it consists of the four [Buddhas] beginning with Vajradharma, who rely upon the discriminating wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) characterized by the transformation of the conceptualizing mind (*vikalpamanas*).

The discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), which is characterized by the transformation of the conceptualizing mind, is precisely the discernment of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) because it is free from the aforementioned distortions; furthermore, it is the cause for never turning back from the naturally pure *dharmatā*, from insight (*prajñā*), and from primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), and for the thorough knowledge of the entirety of the intended meaning.

The emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) is due to the lack of volitional construction (*anabhisaṃskāra*) regarding the form-body (*rūpakāya*), which consists of the primary marks and secondary signs.
The emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*) is due to the non-construction of those dharmas whose intrinsic nature consists of the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, and so forth.
The emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*) is due to the non-superimposition of a person (*pudgala*) or of phenomena (*dharma*).

The emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence [is so called] because of the non-denial of the characteristics of emptiness as they have been described, and because of the absence of volitional construction.

Therefore, one is the embodiment of the four [deities], such as Vajradharma, who rely upon the wisdom of all-accomplishing action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). This wisdom of all-accomplishing action, which is the nature of the transformed bases of the visual consciousness and so forth, consists—by way of abandoning the aforementioned distortions—in making offerings to all the Sugatas without exception, protecting them from all sides, and clearing away obstacles.
Because the body and so forth are the very cause of the primordial wisdom of emptiness.

Likewise, by virtue of being the very antidotes to stinginess, immoral conduct, intolerance, and laziness, they are themselves the nature of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence.

Therefore, it is the nature of the four secret offerings; for, in their respective order, the accomplishment of mirror-like wisdom and the others consists in producing the specific qualities of spontaneous presence through the power of the purification of one's own doors of liberation.

That very [nature] consists of the fourfold nature of external offerings—characterized by the perfections of meditative concentration, wisdom, aspiration, and skillful means—by way of abandoning distraction, impaired wisdom, unreal aspirations, and unskillful means;
for its very essence is the engagement with the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) through joy, by means of the path involving effort.

By their very nature as faith, diligence, mindfulness, and meditative concentration, they constitute the four guardians who protect the four gates; for they are the causes of great conviction, engagement, joy, and continuity regarding the Great Vehicle of the Mahāyāna.

In relation to the mere purity of that very wisdom, it consists of the sixteen meditative absorptions (samādhi) such as loving-kindness (maitrī) and so forth, by way of the distinctions of emptiness as previously explained.
Relying on method alone is the very nature of all mundane meditative concentrations without exception.

Because it is free from the superimposition of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields of affliction, that very reality should be understood as having the characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields of purification.

Having abandoned all superimpositions through a mind that conceptualizes that very reality without exception, one should therefore rely correctly upon it for as long as there is conceptualization of reality; this is because, by means of the very adherence to its intrinsic nature, it serves as the correct basis for its arising, since it is held to be that which produces the primordial wisdom of the yogi.

Having perceived that very reality as non-different from oneself in its entirety, one should offer perfect worship with all objects, such as forms and so forth, which have become the domain of appearance.

If it is argued: "But how can the enjoyment of all desires and so forth by the self alone constitute a form of worship that is a cause of supreme merit? For the enjoyment of forms and other objects by Śrāvakas and others is prohibited as a cause of ruin, since it generates passion and other afflictions," [we reply]: that is not so, because the three realms themselves are what is to be worshipped.

For it is not that an "ātman" distinct from the mind is intended here; nor is there the worshipability of an Īśvara or the like—whose nature is unperceived and whose characteristics are sublated by valid cognition (pramāṇa)—other than the circle of deities (*devatācakra*) characterized as just described, which is nothing but the mind itself. If it is argued: "In that case, even an image or the like, being distinct from the self and possessing the nature of the intended deity, would not be worthy of worship," we reply: that is not so. For even that [image] is superimposed (*adhyāropita*) by means of that very [mind]. There is nothing else existing apart from what appears [to consciousness]; for the superimposition of the deity upon one's own self alone yields the unsurpassed fruit.

As for what was also said—that [the practice] is prohibited because it precludes the enjoyment of Śrāvakas and others—that too is untenable. For a prohibitive statement that functions in a general sense is sublated by a specific injunction; for contradiction would occur between a statement of injunction and a statement of prohibition only when they share the same object, not when they have different objects. This is because, in the case of a Śrāvaka who is attached to external objects and whose mind has not realized the true nature of reality... [the prohibition applies to him].

If it is argued that because there is no difference in the essential nature of what is to be done (*kartavya*), it is untenable for there to be multiple objects [of action], we say: No. This is because [the action] is conducive to production through a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*). For it is undesirable action that is the object of prohibition. Moreover, everything does not become so merely by the determination of its form; for instance, one observes that poison which has been consecrated with mantras lacks the capacity to bring about death.

Thus, in this context, even though physical and other actions motivated by an intention such as compassion might generally be prohibited in another passage as having undesirable results, they are not so here; for example, through acts such as piercing the eyes out of compassion, one produces pain in those persons who are of such a nature. However, for Bodhisattvas, all action produced by virtuous mental orientations such as compassion is within the scope of permission, because that is the very characteristic of the Bodhisattva path.
"There is no offense for one with a virtuous mind, nor for one who acts out of affection and compassion" [from the *Triśaraṇasaptati*].
Likewise,
"even that which is prohibited is permitted for a compassionate person who perceives the greater purpose."
And it is further said:
"Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, everything that arises from the intention of Bodhisattvas becomes entirely auspicious, because their minds are under their own control."

This is because they condemn acts such as taking life when these are separated from skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), whereas for one who is skilled in means, those very acts are permitted. As it is said in the *Trayastriṃśa* and the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*:

In this regard, a bodhisattva completely and in every way abstains from taking life, even when he sees other beings harming the Three Jewels. Likewise, he abstains from taking what is not given, even when he sees other beings who are impoverished. Similarly, regarding the wives of others and those belonging to another, he does not even conceive the thought of soliciting them, much less proceed to embrace them or engage in the union of the two organs; except, as it is explained in detail, in such cases where it is a necessary duty.
The distinction regarding all "crests" (*śikhā*) should be understood as follows:

bodily and vocal action motivated by an intention for gain and so forth is unwholesome (*akuśala*) because its fruit is undesirable, yet it is not so by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), since its intrinsic character (*svabhāva*) is neutral (*avyākṛta*). However, that which is manifested by an intention directed toward the benefit of others brings about unsurpassed fruit; therefore, it has the nature of a Bodhisattva’s crest. Furthermore, a Bodhisattva would not be blameworthy (*sāvadya*) if he were to protect and maintain his own livelihood.

As the Blessed One said: "That which is the source of the qualities of awakening for those who are certain in the Dharma—this is the purpose of the ethical discipline of those endowed with virtuous qualities. That which causes the decline of the qualities of awakening for those who act for the benefit [of others]—this is called 'immoral conduct' by the Leaders.
And as it is said in the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa*:
"Without feeling revulsion toward any of the skillful means."

For even when the enjoyment of objects and so forth is equal, the distinction between what is faulty and what is faultless is established by virtue of one's underlying intention (*adhyāśaya*). For one who possesses afflicted attachment, the enjoyment of objects is afflicted; however, for one whose intention is unafflicted, it is unafflicted—thus everything is clear.

That [mental engagement] is also threefold: that which accords with worldly results, that which accords with one's own nirvāṇa, and that which accords with the unsurpassed result. Among these, the first is the mental engagement that, for the sake of attaining higher realms and so forth, correctly applies itself to the objects as they are attained, such as the gods and so on.

The second [type] seeks the enlightenment of the śrāvakas and so forth; it consists of the individual discernment of form and so on in terms of their impermanence and other characteristics within the context of suchness. As it is said in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*:

"Monks, when a monk sees forms with the eye, he overcomes the forms; he is not overcome by the forms," and so on, up to: "because he dwells having perceived them as impermanent, for that reason he is not overcome by the forms"—this is what was taught in detail. Regarding the third [point], there are also four aspects.

Engaging through devotion to aspiration prayers; engaging through the individual investigation of reality alone; engaging through the focal object of mere vastness; and engaging through both profundity and vastness.

In that regard, for those who have attained the appearance of forms and so forth, there is a primary orientation toward the mental state that brings about benefit for all beings without exception, following from the direct experience of their own essential nature.

Regarding the complete purity of the sphere of activity, when a bodhisattva here sees a form that is a basis for mental pleasure with his eye, he should likewise generate the thought: "May all sentient beings attain the supreme body of a Tathāgata!"

When seeing those who have become objects of mental unease, one should generate the thought: "May all sentient beings become weary of the suffering of saṃsāra. When seeing those who have become objects of equanimity, one should generate the thought: "May all sentient beings attain mental equanimity toward all phenomena. Thus it is taught at length.

Thus, it is also stated in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*: "In whatever way the Compassionate One engages in his own conduct within the sphere of the senses, in that very way he manifests himself before sentient beings, abiding in accordance with what is appropriate for each."

The second is the mental engagement of the discernment of selflessness (*nairātmya-vicāra-manaskāra*) regarding all objects of enjoyment, characterized by compassion and regard for the realm of sentient beings. As the Blessed One said: "O son of noble family, for the sake of creating obstacles for that Dharma-preaching monk, Māra the Evil One may manifest forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and..."

It has been taught in detail that those objects of attachment which have been pointed out here should be fully utilized after having been overwhelmed by skillful means and wisdom; for the mental engagement with reality (*tattva-manasikāra*) is the very antidote to the arising of every single fault. This is because even the performance of undesirable actions is diminished and exhausted through the individual investigation of reality.

By its power, the capacity to produce the fruit of desire is obstructed; yet, for one who has realized form and so forth as being of the nature of correct individual investigation, what opportunity remains for afflicted karma?

Afflicted karma, which is a particular state of a distorted mind, does not arise simultaneously [with the discernment of selflessness], because it is incompatible with that discernment of selflessness. As it has been said: "The variety of the world is not what is desired; rather, the desire for a person's conceptualization is what is desired. Although the variety of the world remains as such,"

It is said: "Even those who are steadfast should abandon desire for this. Thirdly, because it focuses on the vast [object], even one's own internal forms and so forth serve as the antidote to attachment toward ordinary forms; thus, they are the indirect cause for establishing one in the state of perfect buddhahood.

This is because one enjoys the forms and so forth that accord with the pride of the nature of a perfect Buddha. If that were the case, even so, one might object: "In that case, the Blessed One’s thorough meditation on his own nature is not itself the nature of a perfect Buddha from the perspective of ultimate truth."

In that case, there would be no purification of the ordinary self either, because in reality form and so forth do not exist at all. This is similar to the teaching that those forms and so forth which are made into objects through the attachment, "I see form and so forth," do not exist in reality in that way.

Therefore, according to the Blessed One, some forms of attachment that do not depend on abiding in suchness are non-virtuous because they give rise to what is undesirable, whereas the other is virtuous because it is necessary for the goal of the supreme person.

This is seen from the treatise. For that very reason, it is established that even by way of mere designation, the pride of being a Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*) is the cause for bringing about the supreme excellence; however, it cannot be established that everything becomes virtuous in nature merely through the personal enjoyment [of that status].

This is because, through the power of intention, that [act] is also of a virtuous nature. Suppose some bodhisattva were to provide all the necessities for comfort to each of eighty thousand tathāgatas, together with their retinues of eighty thousand bhikṣus, for many eons over a period of eight hundred thousand years; yet another bodhisattva were to fully uphold the sublime Dharma.
It is said that if, for that reason, one were to enjoy alms oneself, this bodhisattva would generate much more merit than the former.

The fourth conceptualization is that which is directed toward performing the welfare of all beings without exception through the emanation of various transformations that have perfectly emerged from the gateway of manifold rays of light, having the nature of the Sugata’s body because it has abandoned every trace of the defilement of conceptualizing its own intrinsic nature; this conforms to the aforementioned forms and so forth.

The view that all things without exception are equal, distinguished as described above, is the supreme cause for singular perfection, because it takes as its object the very nature of that which is to be realized through direct perception.

The mere apprehension of doubt regarding the presence of a transgression in the worship of the Perfect Buddha—which consists of investigating such forms as visible matter (*rūpa*) and so forth in an indeterminate manner—is not itself a cause for a great transgression.

Because this is the very antidote to ordinary, distorted mental engagement (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), it constitutes the nature of the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*). Because it is the basis for supreme *nirvāṇa* through the cessation of all mental engagements toward the unreal objects of the eyes and so forth, it has the sense of being the supreme restraint (*saṃvara*). Thus it is said:
"Restraint of the eye is excellent; restraint of the ear is excellent."
Restraint through the nose is good; restraint through the tongue is good;
restraint through the body is good; restraint through the mind is good.
A monk who is restrained in every way is liberated from all suffering.

Thus it was said. Because one perceives both oneself and others as being of the nature of a perfect Buddha, this pertains to the essence of the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*); yet, because there is no error regarding its own nature, it does not even perceive the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).

In the same way, one should understand—following the previous [explanation]—that all the perfections and so forth are entirely subsumed within the very act of turning away from faults such as avarice.

Therefore, those who have turned away from the nature that is concordant with the generation of such a bodhicitta have abandoned the supreme cause and will not become vessels for perfect enlightenment. Fear regarding what is not the proper basis is itself the very cause that produces a fruitless lineage:
"Whosoever, through the cause of delusion, becomes afraid of what is not the proper basis..."
Because a great mass of merit will not arise over a long period of time,
those who lack noble lineage, lack friends, have not trained their minds,
and have not cultivated virtue in the past will become terrified of these teachings and will fall away from this great purpose.
Supreme enlightenment is for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others; it possesses manifold radiance, and its sole cause is this very mind, which is equal to that [enlightenment].
By even a small portion of the stainless merit arising from my having explained this,
may beings with minds free from delusion regarding the wisdom of the Buddha attain enlightenment.
This concludes the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra* (Introduction to the Realization of the Self), composed by the master Buddhajñānapāda.
